posts.title: “Did you know...” about ethnobotany.
posts.description: Ethnobotany studies how cultures have used plants for medicine, food and rituals. Many current remedies come from ancestral knowledge - every plant has a story to discover! 🌱💡

pill.title: CONTENTS
pill.content:
1. Introduction to ethnobotany and its importance in human cultures.
2. The relationship between plants and ancestral civilizations throughout time.
3. The traditional knowledge of indigenous peoples about plants and their use.
4. Medicinal plants: myths, realities and scientific validations.
5. Ethnobotany as a tool for biodiversity conservation.
6. Sacred plants and their role in the rituals of diverse cultures. 
7. The role of shamans and healers in transmitting ethnobotanical knowledge.

pill.title: Introduction (Welcome to the world of ethnobotany).
pill.content:
“Did you know that Colombia, one of the most biodiverse countries in the world is home to thousands of plant species with traditional uses documented by indigenous communities?”.

Ethnobotany studies the ancestral use of plants in everyday life, highlighting their medicinal, nutritional, symbolic and cultural value. This knowledge, transmitted orally, is key to the identity of indigenous, Afro-descendant and peasant communities in Colombia and Latin America. In this pill, you will discover curiosities, surprising stories and concrete examples of the traditional use of plants in our country, highlighting the connection between nature and culture.

pill.title: THEMATIC DEVELOPMENT
pill.content: Ethnobotany studies the ancestral use of plants as medicine, food and cultural symbol, being key to the identity of indigenous, Afro-descendant and peasant communities in Colombia. Promoted by Richard Evans Schultes, considered the “Father of Ethnobotany”, who investigated in the Colombian Amazon the use of medicinal and hallucinogenic plants by peoples such as the Tukano and the Witoto, this discipline values the botanical knowledge of more than 80 ethnic groups and promotes respect for cultural and natural heritage.

pill.title: Thematic Development (Relationship between plants and ancestral cultures).
pill.content: Pre-Columbian cultures developed systems for the use and classification of plants that still exist today. The Muiscas used fique to make rope, coca in sacred rituals and corn as the staple of their diet. In the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, the Kogui and Arhuacos see plants as spiritual beings that teach and protect, valuing them for both their physical and symbolic properties.

pill.title: Thematic Development (Indigenous wisdom and traditional use of plants).
pill.content: Indigenous communities integrate the natural and the spiritual, attributing to each plant a spirit and a purpose. For example, Yagé (Ayahuasca) is seen as a master plant that teaches and guides through visions. Knowledge about its use is transmitted through rituals and chants. In Colombia, more than 6,000 species of traditional use have been recorded, many not yet studied by science, but this ancestral knowledge is at risk due to the loss of languages and western influence.

pill.title: Thematic Development (Medicinal plants: myths and realities).
Thematic Development (Ethnobotany and biodiversity conservation).
pill.content: Colombia, the second most biodiverse country in the world, is home to a large part of its flora in indigenous and peasant territories. Conserving these territories also protects traditional knowledge. Ethnobotany documents this knowledge before it disappears, especially in communities where elders are the sole bearers of this knowledge.  Initiatives such as ethnobotanical gardens, seed banks and environmental education, like the Ethnobotanical Garden of the SINCHI Institute in Leticia, Amazonas, help preserve this legacy.

pill.title: Thematic Development (Sacred plants in different cultures).
pill.content: Indigenous spirituality is closely linked to plants, seen as “spirit beings” that aid in healing and connection with the divine. In Colombia, sacred plants such as coca, sweet yucca and yagé are used in rituals of healing and connection with the ancestors. In ceremonies such as the Kogui “mambeada”, coca is chewed in spiritual reflections. These practices, linked to the respect and care of plants, are now recognized as intangible cultural heritage.

pill.title: Thematic Development (Healers, shamans and the transmission of knowledge).
pill.content: In many Colombian communities, knowledge of plants is possessed by elders known as sabedores, curanderos or shamans, who learn as children guided by dreams and ancestral teachings. In the Uitoto culture, for example, they “ask” permission from the forest before collecting a plant. Although the figure of the healer was stigmatized, today its value is recognized as a living heritage, whose preservation requires intercultural dialogue and recognition of indigenous rights.

pill.title: Conclusion (Conclusions about the pill).
pill.content:
Ethnobotany reminds us that knowledge about plants is not only scientific, but also cultural and spiritual. Through the study of plants and their traditional uses, we better understand the history, medicine and identity of peoples. Preserving this ancestral knowledge is vital to face current challenges such as biodiversity loss and the search for sustainable solutions.
Valuing indigenous wisdom and promoting dialogue between science and tradition opens up new possibilities for a future that is more conscious and respectful of nature.

posts.title: Useful and Common Plants
posts.description: Plants have been fundamental allies in everyday life. From medicinal herbs to essential ingredients in the kitchen, many species provide us with incredible benefits. Discover here some of the most commonly used plants and their multiple uses in health, food and wellness. 🌱✨

pill.title: CONTENTS
pill.content:
1. Introduction: the plant wealth of Tame, Yopal and Saravena.
2. The historical relationship of plants with the life of the llanera.
3. Useful plants in medicine, food and construction.
4. Myths and realities about plants in the llanera culture.
5. Conservation of useful species in Casanare and Arauca.
6. Sacred plants: connection between nature and spirituality. 
7. Knowers and guardians: the transmission of knowledge about plants.

pill.title: Introduction.
pill.content: Colombia is a country of great biodiversity, and within its regions, the Eastern Plains - with municipalities such as Tame, Yopal and Saravena - are home to plants that have accompanied communities since ancient times. These are used not only as food or medicine, but also in rituals, constructions and cultural practices. To know them is to understand the history and identity of the region.

pill.title: Thematic Development (What are useful plants?).
pill.content:
Useful plants have been used to cover basic needs such as health, food and culture. In municipalities such as Tame, Yopal and Saravena, traditional species are used:

  • Moriche (Mauritia flexuosa): yields sweet fruits, juices and fibers for roofing and handicrafts.
  • Matarratón (Gliricidia sepium): used in fences, as shade and as a remedy for bites.
  • Cují (Prosopis juliflora): its wood is firewood, its fruits feed animals and its thorns delimit land.
  • Guásimo (Guazuma ulmifolia): leaves for stomach ailments and fruits for beverages.

These plants have allowed the llaneros to adapt to the savannah and rivers.

pill.title: THEMATIC DEVELOPMENT
pill.content:
The plain has taught its inhabitants to see plants as life companions. For example:

  • Moriche: its palms are used as cool roofs, ideal for the hot climate of Tame and Saravena.
  • Guásimo: its boiled fruits relieve coughs and respiratory problems.
  • Uña de Gato (Cat's Claw): collected in the trails and used as an infusion to strengthen defenses.

Each plant in the plains teaches to live with respect and balance with nature.

pill.title: THEMATIC DEVELOPMENT
pill.content:
The knowledge of useful plants comes from the experience of grandmothers, grandfathers and wise men who have observed nature for generations.

Some plants and their traditional uses:

  • Caruto (Genipa americana): its fruits serve as a natural dye, and its leaves as a healing infusion.
  • Bledo (Amaranthus sp.): nutritious leaves used in soups and stews.
  • Leucaena (Leucaena leucocephala): forage tree and source of organic fertilizer.
  • Sarrapia (Dipteryx odorata): its seed produces a sweet aroma used in perfumes and home remedies.


This knowledge is still alive in the villages where the connection with the land is still a daily occurrence.

pill.title: Thematic Development (Myths and realities).
pill.content:
In the plains they say: “if it's bush, it's good”, but not all plants are harmless. For example:

  • Borrachero (Brugmansia): common in gardens, has dangerous psychotropic properties if used without knowledge.
  • Matarratón: useful as a fence and repellent, but badly prepared it can intoxicate.
  • Yopo: seed used in indigenous rituals that induces visions; should only be used with spiritual guidance.

This knowledge is key to self-care and rural survival.

pill.title: Thematic Development (Ethnobotany and biodiversity conservation).
pill.content:
Cattle ranching, intensive agriculture and urbanization have reduced the useful plants in Tame, Yopal and Saravena.

But there are initiatives that seek to protect them:

  • Community and school nurseries: teach children and young people how to grow and care for plants.
  • Home gardens and model farms: combine basic crops with medicinal and forage plants.
  • Moriche recovery and reforestation: help conserve water and biodiversity.

Preserving them is essential to care for nature and maintain traditions.

pill.title: Thematic Development (Sacred plants: identity and spirituality).
THEMATIC DEVELOPMENT
pill.content:
The “sabedores” are people who have dedicated their lives to knowing the plants, their cycles and their uses. In farms, roads and villages of Tame, Yopal and Saravena, these people:
- They know in which moon each plant is harvested.
- They know where and when useful species sprout.
- They teach young people and children to respect the natural environment.

They are a living memory that protects a knowledge that not only takes care of people, but also of the land.

pill.title: CONCLUSIONS
pill.content:
Useful plants are part of the essence of life in the plains. To learn about them is to know the roots of Tame, Yopal and Saravena, where nature teaches lessons of respect, wisdom and sustainability every day.
Preserving these plants and their knowledge is to ensure a future where communities and their territories can live in balance.

posts.title: Conservation and awareness
posts.description: The wisdom of ancient cultures has taught us the value of plants and their importance in our lives. Today, more than ever, it is essential to protect this knowledge and the ecosystems that sustain it. Through the conservation and rescue of endangered species, we can ensure that future generations will continue to benefit from the natural and cultural wealth that surrounds us. 🌎✨

pill.title: CONTENTS
pill.content:
1. Introduction: Plant and cultural biodiversity of the Orinoco.
2. Living history: useful plants in the Eastern Plains.
3. Traditional uses: health, food and peasant practices.
4. Current threats: oblivion, deforestation and loss of knowledge.
5. Local actions for conservation in Casanare and Arauca.
6. Guardians of the territory: wise men and women of the Llano. 
7. Conclusion and call to action from the Orinoco Biodiversa Foundation.

pill.title: Introduction.
pill.content:
The Orinoco is one of the richest regions in Colombia in terms of biological and cultural diversity. Municipalities such as Tame, Saravena and Paz de Ariporo have a great variety of key plants for peasant, indigenous and llanero life.                                                                       
Fundación Orinoquía Biodiversa works to protect these species and the traditional knowledge that accompanies them.

Ethnobotany recognizes that wisdom also flourishes with plants. Each leaf and root tells stories of resistance, adaptation and care of the territory.

pill.title: Desarrollo Temático (Historia viva: plantas y pueblos del llano).
pill.content:
In the Eastern Plains, the relationship with plants goes beyond the material. They are part of daily life, grandmother's knowledge and the secrets of the forest. Examples:

  • Moriche: palm that offers shade, food, material and is a symbol of life for riverside communities.
  • Matarratón: living fence, medicine for animals and natural repellent.
  • Guásimo: tree of roads and patios, used in drinks that relieve coughs and digestive problems.

Fundación Orinoquía Biodiversa supports the registration of this knowledge and community strengthening in rural areas of Arauca and Casanare.

pill.title: Desarrollo Temático (Usos tradicionales: salud, alimentación y prácticas rurales).
Thematic Development (Current threats: oblivion, deforestation and loss of knowledge).
pill.content:
In the highlands and foothills, many useful plants disappear due to:

  • Livestock and agro-industrial expansion.
  • Contamination of water sources.
  • Rural migration and youth disinterest.
  • Stigmatization of ancestral knowledge.

When a knower is lost, knowledge is also lost. FOB promotes community actions to protect this knowledge and unite tradition with science.

pill.title: Thematic Development (Community actions for conservation).
pill.content:
Fundación Orinoquía Biodiversa promotes education and conservation processes with an ethnobotanical approach:

  • School gardens to teach about traditional plants.
  • Community nurseries in peasant farms.
  • Ethnobotanical gardens and seed banks.
  • Awareness campaigns on the responsible use of plants.

These actions strengthen cultural and food sovereignty and care for the territory.

pill.title: Thematic Development (Guardians of the territory: wise men and women).
pill.content:
The savants of the plains not only know the bush: they dialogue with it. They recognize plants by their smell, leaves and flowering. They are who:

  • They know where to find the right plant.
  • They teach by word and example.
  • They accompany births, rituals and healings.

FOB supports the strengthening of their role as pillars of peace and territorial sustainability.

question.question: Moriche is a palm used only as an ornamental palm in gardens.

pill.title: CONCLUSIONS
pill.content:
Ethnobotany is not only memory: it is collective action. It is an invitation to look at the forest with different eyes, to see in each plant a piece of history and a seed for the future.
At Fundación Orinoquía Biodiversa we believe that conservation is also education, research, planting and walking with the community. Because every time we sow a traditional plant, we also sow dignity, knowledge and resistance.

Conservation is memory. Culture is biodiversity. Ethnobotany is hope.
